theme: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel
enonce_markdown: In Genesis 22, God tells Abraham to offer Isaac on a mountain in the land of Moriah. When Abraham is stopped by the angel of the Lord, what does he find that he offers instead of his son?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Read the narrative closely: the answer is in the closing verses of the episode.

### Solution

In Genesis 22:13 Abraham looks up and sees a ram caught in a thicket by its horns, and he offers it as a burnt offering in place of Isaac. The other animals are not mentioned in this scene.

choix.texte: A lamb brought by his servants from the camp
A ram caught by its horns in a thicket
A young goat sent by Sarah
A dove and a pigeon provided by Isaac

theme: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel
enonce_markdown: The name Israel was first given to Jacob after which event?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Match each name change to the narrative in which the text places it.

### Solution

In Genesis 32:22-32 Jacob wrestles through the night at the Jabbok. The figure tells him that he will no longer be called Jacob but Israel, because he has striven with God and with men. The ladder dream (Genesis 28), the sale of the birthright (Genesis 25) and the service for Rachel (Genesis 29) all come before this event and none of them is the occasion of the new name.

choix.texte: He dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven at Bethel
He bought Esau's birthright for a meal of stew
He worked seven years for Rachel in Haran
He wrestled with a mysterious figure at the river Jabbok until daybreak

theme: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel
enonce_markdown: In Genesis 17 God changes Abram's name to Abraham. According to the text, the new name expresses that Abraham will be:
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In the patriarchal narratives a name change is explained by the text itself. Use the explanation that the passage gives, not a later tradition.

### Solution

Genesis 17:5 says: Abram becomes Abraham because God has made him the father of a multitude of nations. The laughter theme belongs to the name Isaac (Genesis 17:17 and 21:6), and striving with God belongs to the name Israel (Genesis 32). The title 'friend of God' is a later description of Abraham and is not the explanation given for the name in Genesis 17.

choix.texte: The father of a multitude of nations
The friend of God among the nations
The one who laughs at God's promise
The one who strives with God and with men

theme: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel
enonce_markdown: In the covenant ceremony of Genesis 15, animals are cut in two and the pieces are laid opposite one another. Who or what passes between the pieces?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Ask who takes the oath in an ancient covenant ceremony of this kind, and who is shown acting in the text.

### Solution

In Genesis 15:12-17 Abram falls into a deep sleep, and a smoking fire pot and a flaming torch pass between the pieces. The passage presents God alone as binding himself to the promise of descendants and land, while Abram remains passive. Neither Abram, Sarai nor Eliezer passes between the animals.

choix.texte: Abram alone, carrying the knife of sacrifice
Abram and Sarai together, as the two parties bound by the oath
A smoking fire pot and a flaming torch, representing God, while Abram is in a deep sleep
Eliezer of Damascus, acting as Abram's representative

theme: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel
enonce_markdown: Examine two ways in which the account of the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22) tests Abraham's faith. [10 marks]
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

State what the text asks of the character, then link each element of the test to a theme of faith (trust, obedience, hope in a promise) with a reference.

### Solution

**Point 1: the cost of the command.** Isaac is described as Abraham's only son, whom he loves (Genesis 22:2). He is also the son through whom God had promised descendants (Genesis 17:19-21). To obey, Abraham must be ready to give up the person on whom the promise depended, so the test touches both his love and his hope.

**Point 2: obedience without full knowledge.** Abraham rises early and sets out without argument (22:3). His answer to Isaac, 'God will provide the lamb' (22:8), shows trust that God will act, even though he does not know how. The Letter to the Hebrews (11:17-19) later reads this as faith that God could even raise the dead.

**Resolution.** The angel stops Abraham, a ram is provided, and God renews the promise of descendants and of blessing for all nations (22:15-18), because Abraham 'did not withhold his son'. The episode shows that faith in these narratives means trust in God's word at the point of greatest cost.

A complete answer states the two points above, supports each with a reference, and ends with the divine response.

theme: A Level Religious Studies - patriarchs of israel
enonce_markdown: 'The patriarchal narratives show that God's promises depend on his grace and not on human worthiness.' Using the lives of Abraham and Jacob, assess this statement. [25 marks]
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Define the claim, give evidence for it from each patriarch, give evidence that human response also matters, then reach a reasoned judgement.

### Solution

**Introduction.** The statement says that the promises of land, descendants and blessing were fulfilled because of God's initiative and fidelity, not because the patriarchs deserved them.

**Evidence in favour.**
- Abraham is called while living in a setting that, in the account, does not know the Lord (Genesis 11-12); he does nothing to earn the call.
- Abraham fails at times: he passes Sarai off as his sister in Egypt (Genesis 12:10-20) and he has a child with Hagar to hasten the promise (Genesis 16). The promise is still renewed (Genesis 15 and 17).
- Jacob is chosen before birth (Genesis 25:23) and, although he deceives Esau and Isaac (Genesis 27), he receives the promise at Bethel (Genesis 28:13-15).

**Evidence that human response matters.** Abraham 'believed the Lord' (Genesis 15:6) and obeyed in the call and in Genesis 22, after which the promise is reaffirmed 'because you have obeyed my voice' (22:18). Jacob suffers consequences of his conduct (flight, deception by Laban) and is changed at the Jabbok (Genesis 32).

**Judgement.** The narratives emphasise grace in the initiative and the continuation of the promise, but they present faith and obedience as the response expected of the patriarchs and show them facing consequences. The statement is largely justified if 'depend' means the source of the promise, and less so if it means that conduct is irrelevant.
